catalog_quote: Le mofu-nord, de la famille tchadique, est une langue à registre. A cet effet, l'on a trois tons ponctuels: Le ton haut [´] [wájáŋ]: "marigot" / Le ton moyen [¯] [bābā]: "père" / Le ton bas [`] [hàjàhà]: "bon". La fonction lexicale. La langue n'est constituée que d'un seul type d'opposition; l'opposition lexicale. (p. 31) ... il n'en est pas le cas en mofu-nord. Les tons grammaticaux sont inexistants. (p. 32) ... En mofu-nord, la voyelle /a/ s'élide lorsqu'elle apparaît dans un environnement où la syllabe qu'elle précède est accentuée. Il est à noter que c'est un processus peu courant dans cette langue. (p. 34) ... L'accentuation est l'élévation ou augmentation d'intensité de la voix dans la prononciation d'une syllabe. L'analyse de ce processus dans la langue nous a été suggérée par le professeur Mutaka. (p. 35) ... Ainsi, [aj] et [ej] deviennent [i] lorsque le mot qui les porte en finale est suivi d'un autre mot. Cette règle s'applique à tous les mots se terminant par [aj] ou [ej] qui sont employés dans l'énoncé. Mais en isolation ces morphèmes gardent leur terminaison initiale. (p. 35) ... Bref, selon la proposition de Mutaka, ej, aj et aw se trouvent en position accentuée et se réduisent en i (pour aj et ej) et en u (pour aw) en position non accentuée. (p. 37)
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: North Mofu (nort3046) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Hollingsworth 1990 'A study of tone, stress and intonation in Mofu-Gudur', is a SIL Cameroon manuscript that Glottolog assigns only to the sister language Mofu-Gudur [mif] mofu1248, so it is other-language for this key; no open copy was found (not in LDH/PuRe, not on archive.org, no DOI; sil.org, silcam.org, OLAC and the Internet Archive could not be reached by automated download) — priority low here, high for mofu1248. The only first-hand description of North Mofu, Abdou 2004 (open at MPG PuRe, held by the project), states a three-tone register system with lexical tone only and invokes 'accent' (intensity) solely as an utterance-final conditioning environment for aj/ej/aw reduction and /a/-elision, with no word-stress placement rule; Barreteau 1983 (Mofu-Gudur, held by the project, pp. 373-374) describes the sister language's non-distinctive 'accent d'intensité' on the last syllable before pause. Everything downloaded and the verbatim locators are logged in

new_statements.translation: Mofu-North, of the Chadic family, is a register [tone] language. Accordingly there are three level tones [high, mid, low] […] The language has only one type of opposition: the lexical opposition. (p. 31) […] Accentuation is the raising or increase of the intensity of the voice in the pronunciation of a syllable. The analysis of this process in the language was suggested to us by Professor Mutaka. (p. 35) […] In short, following Mutaka's proposal, ej, aj and aw occur in accented position and reduce to i (for aj and ej) and to u (for aw) in non-accented position. (p. 37)

new_statements.rule_in_words: North Mofu is described as a three-level register tone language (H, M, L; lexical tone only, no grammatical tone). The thesis also invokes an intensity 'accent', but only as a conditioning factor in two morphophonological rules and without a general placement rule: word-final [aj]/[ej]/[aw] count as being in 'accented position' when the word is pronounced in isolation (utterance-final) and as 'non-accented' when another word follows in the utterance (where they reduce to i/u); and /a/ elides before an accented syllable (màjá 'mère' > màj-daw 'sa mère'). Read literally this makes the accent a pre-pausal, phrase-final prominence rather than a fixed word-level stress.
new_statements.exceptions: /a/-elision is 'un processus peu courant' (rare); reduction 'applies to all words ending in [aj] or [ej] used in an utterance', but 'en isolation ces morphèmes gardent leur terminaison initiale'; the reduction also occurs before the plural suffix -haj (tápàj 'bâton' > tápi-haj). The accent analysis is attributed to a personal communication (Mutaka), not to instrumental or systematic evidence.
new_statements.domain_note: Accent is defined by position in the utterance, not in the word: a word's final syllable is 'accented' when the word is utterance-final / in citation form and 'non-accented' when followed by another word. Data are nominals elicited from a 223-item questionnaire, reference informant a native of Douroum.
new_statements.identity_note: Abdou 2004 describes 'mofu-nord' = ALCAM 173, spoken in the cantons Douroum, Douvangar and Wazang (plus Mbozo) of Méri arrondissement, Diamaré, Far North Cameroon; reference informant a native of Douroum (Glottolog dialect Douroun dour1242), with variation cross-checked against Douvangar and Wazang (Wazan waza1238) speakers. This matches Glottolog nort3046 / ISO mfk. Warning: the 'Mofou-Nord' canton named in Barreteau 1983 (p. 6) is Mokong, part of Mofu-Gudur [mif] mofu1248 — a different language; the Barreteau 1978, Hollingsworth 2002/2004 and Pohlig 1992 items attached to nort3046 in our source list are all Mofu-Gudur works, and Glottolog itself assigns only Abdou 2004 (plus ethnographic/wordlist items) to North Mofu.

new_statements.reading: North Mofu is described as a three-level register tone language (H, M, L) with lexical tone only. 'Accent' (intensity) is introduced only as a conditioning environment for vowel elision and for the reduction of word-final aj/ej/aw: the final syllable counts as accented when the word stands alone (utterance-final) and as unaccented when another word follows. This is phrase/utterance-final prominence, not a lexical word-stress placement rule; no such rule is stated anywhere in the thesis. It matches Barreteau's Mofu-Gudur analysis of a non-distinctive 'accent d'intensité' on the last syllable before pause. Coding suggestion if the language is added: tone language, no lexical word stress (prominence = pre-pausal final syllable).

sources.note: Ch. II 'Rappel phonologique' (pp. 13-38): Mofu-North is a register tone language with three level tones H/M/L, lexical function only, no grammatical tones (pp. 31-33). 'Accentuation' (intensity) is introduced ad hoc on Prof. Mutaka's suggestion to condition /a/-elision and reduction of word-final aj/ej/aw: these are 'en position accentuée' when the word stands alone (utterance-final) and 'non accentuée' when another word follows (pp. 34-37). No general rule of word-stress placement is stated.
